topics.title: Trigonometry 2
topics.subject: mathematics
outcomes: determine trigonometric ratios of angles greater than 90°. (u s)
use the graphs of trigonometric functions to determine values of sine, cosine and tangent for any angle. (u s)
apply sine and cosine rules to solve real life problems. (k u s)

body.text: Surveyors who plan roads between towns cannot always make a right angle. Clock hands open to angles bigger than 90°. In Trigonometry I you used sine, cosine and tangent in right-angled triangles. In this topic you will extend them to any angle, and use the sine and cosine rules to solve any triangle.

Recall the unit circle. It is a circle of radius 1 with its centre at the origin. Turn a radius anticlockwise from the positive x-axis through an angle θ. The end of the radius is the point (cos θ, sin θ). This works for any angle, not just angles below 90°.

body.speech: tan theta equals sin theta over cos theta

body.text: The axes split the circle into four quadrants. The signs of x and y in each quadrant give the signs of the ratios.

items: First quadrant, 0° to 90°: sin, cos and tan are all positive.
Second quadrant, 90° to 180°: only sin is positive.
Third quadrant, 180° to 270°: only tan is positive.
Fourth quadrant, 270° to 360°: only cos is positive.

body.text: To find a ratio of a large angle, first find the acute angle it makes with the x-axis. Then use the quadrant to decide the sign. For an angle in the second quadrant, the acute angle is 180° − θ.

body.speech: sin of, 180 degrees minus theta, equals sin theta
cos of, 180 degrees minus theta, equals minus cos theta

body.title: Find the ratios of 150°
steps: Its acute angle with the x-axis is 180° − 150° = 30°.
Check each value on a calculator.

body.text: The graphs of sine, cosine and tangent

The graph of y = sin θ from 0° to 360° is a smooth wave. It rises from 0 to 1 at 90°, falls to −1 at 270° and returns to 0 at 360°. The graph of y = cos θ is the same wave moved 90° to the left, so it starts at 1. The graph of y = tan θ repeats every 180° and breaks at 90° and 270°, where cos θ = 0.

The graphs show that one value of sine comes from two angles between 0° and 360°. A horizontal line at y = 0.5 cuts the sine wave at 30° and at 150°. In the same way, to solve cos θ = −0.5, a calculator gives 120°. Cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants, and the acute angle is 60°. So θ = 120° or θ = 180° + 60° = 240°.

The sine rule and the cosine rule work in any triangle, not only right-angled ones. Label the corners with capital letters A, B and C. The side opposite each corner gets the matching small letter a, b or c.

body.speech: a over sin A equals b over sin B equals c over sin C

body.text: Use the sine rule when you know one side and the angle opposite it, plus one other side or angle.

body.title: Distance from a health centre to a village
steps: Two health centres, P and Q, are 12 km apart on a straight road near Gulu. A village R is off the road. Angle RPQ = 48° and angle RQP = 65°. Find the distance PR.
Angle PRQ = 180° − 48° − 65° = 67°. PQ is opposite this angle, and PR is opposite the 65° angle.
By the sine rule, PR ÷ sin 65° = 12 ÷ sin 67°.

body.text: Use the cosine rule when you know two sides and the angle between them. It gives the third side.

body.speech: a squared equals b squared plus c squared minus 2 b c cos A

body.text: When you know all three sides, rearrange the rule to find an angle.

body.speech: cos A equals b squared plus c squared minus a squared, all over 2 b c

body.title: The ends of clock hands
steps: The hour hand of a clock is 44 mm long and the minute hand is 57 mm long. The angle between them is 69°. Find the distance d between their ends.

body.title: The angle between two poles
steps: Opio lays two poles, 8.3 m and 11.5 m long, on the ground with one end of each touching. The other two ends are 4.7 m apart. Find the angle between the poles.
The angle we want is opposite the 4.7 m side.

body.title: Clock hands and the cosine rule
body.text: Cut two strips of card, 4.4 cm and 5.7 cm long, and pin them together at one end to make clock hands. Open them to 30°, 60°, 90°, 120° and 150° with a protractor, and measure the distance between the free ends each time. Compare with the cosine rule, and discuss why the values differ slightly.
What happens to the cosine rule a² = b² + c² − 2bc cos A when angle A is 90°? What does this tell you about Pythagoras' theorem?
A calculator gives only one angle for sin⁻¹ 0.5, but the graph shows two angles between 0° and 360°. Why does the calculator choose the one it does?

On the unit circle a point is (cos θ, sin θ), which defines the ratios for any angle. Use the quadrant to fix the sign, and the graphs to find every angle with a given ratio. The sine rule links each side with the sine of its opposite angle. The cosine rule finds a side from two sides and the angle between them, or an angle from three sides.
